isolation.note: Hooks and plugins add processes and connections that are not part of the agent's own behaviour; restricting settings to the project keeps the capture about the harness itself. The override variable replaces the flags when an install needs user settings to authenticate.

tools.note: MultiEdit is in the list so that the step that names it is permitted if this version offers the tool. Version 2.1.296 seems not to (its name appears only among the permission-rule names, beside the retired LS and NotebookRead), and the prompt falls back to Edit in that case. Its controls also run the no-op command in the background and start one subagent that only replies, since the task makes the harness work around a background command (its output file under the harness's temporary directory).

shapes.note: What the 2.1.296 binary says (read from its strings, not measured): the tool executor starts a call while an earlier one still runs only when every running call and the new one are concurrency-safe. Read, Grep, Glob, WebFetch and Agent always are; Write, Edit and NotebookEdit never are; Bash is when its command passes the read-only check (every simple command on an allowlist that includes sleep and cat, no output redirection). So the first block runs concurrently and its first member finishes last, and the second block, whose commands write, runs in claim order. The file tools write through one routine: a sibling temporary file renamed over the target, and, when the temporary cannot be created with EACCES while the target exists (or the rename fails with EXDEV, EPERM, EEXIST or EBUSY), an in-place rewrite of the target (open, truncate, write, fsync, close). A symlinked target is refused, not written in place. The capture script makes locked/ unwritable for every run.
shapes.prompt: Do exactly these six things in order, and nothing else. If a step fails, do not retry it or work around it; go on to the next step. 1) In a single message, make these three tool calls at the same time, in this order: the Bash tool to run exactly: sleep 2; cat slow.txt , then the Bash tool to run exactly: cat fast.txt , then the Read tool on read.txt. 2) In a single message, make these two Bash tool calls at the same time, in this order: one to run exactly: sleep 2; echo one > one.txt , then one to run exactly: echo two > two.txt . 3) Use the Read tool on locked/data.txt. 4) Use the Write tool to overwrite locked/data.txt with the single word direct-one. 5) Use the Edit tool to replace direct-one with direct-two in locked/data.txt. 6) Use the Bash tool to run exactly: cat one.txt two.txt locked/data.txt . Then reply with the single word done.

long.note: Twenty functions times five steps, plus the module checks, the subagent and the build: about 120 calls before any fix, so the model cannot finish early without skipping numbered work it is told is required.
long.prompt: You are working in a small Python package, textkit, in the current directory. Do not use the network. PLAN.md lists 20 functions, numbered 1 to 20, each with a specification file under docs/spec/. The work is finished only when all 20 functions are implemented and tested, CHANGELOG.md has one line per function and make check passes: do not stop before that, and do not skip, merge or reorder steps. Make one tool call per message. Do these steps in order. 1) Use the Glob tool to list docs/spec/*.md, and the Grep tool to search textkit for NotImplementedError. 2) Use the Bash tool to run: make check . It fails, since nothing is implemented yet. 3) For each function in PLAN.md, in order from 1 to 20, one function at a time, do these five steps: a) use the Read tool on its specification file; b) use the Edit tool to replace the raise NotImplementedError line of that function in its module with an implementation that meets the specification; c) use the Edit tool to add at least two unit test methods for it to the test class in the module test file under tests/; d) use the Bash tool to run only that module tests, for example: python3 -m unittest tests.test_strings , and if they fail, fix the code and run them again; e) use the Edit tool to add one line naming the function at the end of CHANGELOG.md. 4) After functions 5, 10, 15 and 20, that is at the end of each module, use the Bash tool to run make check-MODULE for that module (make check-strings, make check-numbers, make check-lists, make check-codec), and use the Grep tool to search that module file for NotImplementedError. 5) Use the Agent tool to start one subagent with exactly this instruction: Use the Glob tool to list tests/test_*.py, use the Bash tool to run: python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t . , then use the Write tool to create REPORT.md stating how many tests ran. Then reply with the single word done. 6) Use the Bash tool to run: make dist , then python3 dist/textkit.pyz slugify "Hello, World" , then python3 dist/textkit.pyz roman 1987 . 7) Use the Read tool on REPORT.md, then use the Edit tool to add a section named Status at the end of README.md saying how many tests pass. 8) Use the Bash tool to run make check a last time. Then reply with the single word done.
long.tools: Read Write Edit Bash Grep Glob Agent

version_lock.note: AGY_CLI_DISABLE_AUTO_UPDATE=true keeps agy's auto-updater from starting a process of its own during a run (the value 1 does not, measured on 1.3.4).

pass_env.why: agy logs in through the session bus

model.note: Passed as --model; the effort is part of the id (-high, -medium, -low, as agy models lists them). The default is the id the existing captures recorded (the user's decision of 2026-10-26).

tool_set.note: A custom agent in the run's workspace lists the task's tools and inherits neither the user's MCP servers nor their customizations (I-24); it is also the settings isolation.

print_timeout.note: agy -p gives up after its print timeout; the long task needs far more than the short ones.

content.reason: agy has none (Go's own TLS), so its connections stay identity-only
